webTitle: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow

fields.headline: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow
fields.trailText: President had brushed away suggestions to slow down AI technology, even as his own party counseled caution
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump on Saturday said he would appoint an artificial intelligence czar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan. As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry. The creation of a czar and a new AI body in the US appears a response to critics of his stance, which in part is born out of a fear that China will best the US in AI development if the industry in America does not continue its rapid growth. However, even many Republicans have been calling for caution and an AI slowdown in the face of its potential threat to public safety. “I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ – Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in a social media post. But in the post, Trump also repeated his stance that the rapidly emerging technology – which some industry experts fear poses a threat to human existence – is being unfairly maligned. Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”. “Over the years, there have been many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country,” he fulminated, including in a list of grievances Russian interference in the 2016 election, Ukraine, global warming, two impeachments, men in women’s sports and “transgender for everyone”. The latest, he wrote, is “the decimation, or destruction, of AI, commonly known as Artificial Intelligence”, and vowed that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”. The president said that any “bad actors” in AI industry could be addressed by criminal and civil systems of justice. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP,” Trump predicted, concluding that the US is “leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way”. The post came after an earlier missive in which he questioned the term “artificial intelligence” – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955 and defined as the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior – to describe the accelerating data-processing revolution now under way. Trump said that “a far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)”. Trump’s proposal comes ahead of his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, next Thursday as the UN general assembly takes place in New York. The US and China are competing for leadership ⁠in the AI sector. The announcement of a planned AI czar also came a day after California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced plans for a panel to develop safety regulations for state’s AI companies that would include the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that become misaligned, or go rogue, from human programmers. As recently as Monday, Trump argued on social media that his administration had done enough to prevent risks of catastrophe. He described calls to slow AI development as part of a “SICK conspiracy” to benefit China. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he wrote. Ahead of the midterm elections, politicians from both political parties are scrambling to find a path to support tech innovation while responding to rising public and industry fears of technological change. The frenzy kicked off earlier this month when a young researcher who had been employed at the AI company Anthropic said AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and even “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. AI executives, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei have since called for a slowdown in the technology’s growth in the wake of an incident in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”. Trump’s call for an AI czar comes after many Republicans have rejected his hands-off approach. Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, has advocated for AI controls, and that state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, has called for laws allowing the state to criminally charge companies for illegal acts carried out with the use of their technologies. Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, has called on Congress to pass AI safety laws and block the sale of high-end technology to China.

webTitle: MS Now, CNN and Politico say reporters have been denied access to White House

fields.headline: MS Now, CNN and Politico say reporters have been denied access to White House
fields.trailText: President said he was banning journalists from those organizations, saying of their coverage: ‘You get sick of it.’
fields.bodyText: Journalists from three US outlets were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning a day after Donald Trump said he would ban them from the executive branch complex in a move that has prompted outrage and shock from free-speech advocates. The outlets were television broadcasters MS Now and CNN as well as the political news website Politico. MS Now said a reporter and a cameraman had been denied access and had their White House press passes confiscated by the US Secret Service at a security gate outside the West Wing. CNN reported that its reporter Betsy Klein was also denied access and had her press pass seized too. Politico said White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett had received the same treatment. “The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS Now said, adding that it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our first amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy”. It said: “We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the president, the administration and the issues that impact the American people.” CNN said in a statement: “We have a right under the US constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.” Politico’s editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, said in a statement to the Politico newsroom: “We stand by [Haslett] and all reporters here covering the White House … We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights.” Trump’s threat to banish CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House has brought condemnation from first amendment advocates and Democratic officials, among others, as the conflict between the US president and parts of the media sharply escalates ahead of November’s midterm elections. It has also thrown into stark relief Trump’s attack on press freedom in the US, which has unnerved civil liberties advocates. In a Truth Social post on Friday afternoon, Trump said he would order the removal of the news outlets “effective immediately” for what he claimed was “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and said he is considering banning more. Trump did not identify a single infraction, but said his decision was “really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it.” The White House Correspondents’ Association, which represents the White House press corps, condemned the move. “The constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” it said on social media. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting or approves of the questions its journalists ask.” The body said the issue is “about more than the rights of journalists” but about “the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office”. Trump has long clashed with the media over what he considers slanted coverage of his administration and himself personally, as well as describing a media environment in which the press and his political opponents are in collusion. Last year the Associated Press was banned form the White House after refusing to acknowledge an executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America. After Friday’s ban was announced, CNN issued a statement saying that removing its reporters from the grounds could violate the law. “CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” a spokesperson for the outlet said. “We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government.” Politico also issued a statement, saying it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones” and “will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them”. Jim Acosta, a former CNN reporter, accused Trump of “taking a meat axe to the free press in this country”. Speaking on MS Now on Friday, Acosta called the latest media bans “a slippery slope” and warned: “We are on the path to having a state media-like system in this country.” Acosta said the media should collectively oppose Trump’s ban. “Each of these news organizations should sue the White House, sue Donald Trump, and that other news organizations in Washington should band together and say, ‘We will not go to the White House and cover you and cover your administration. We’re banning you.’” Press freedom group PEN America said: “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the first amendment works. As we’ve seen time and time again, this administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions. “The White House can’t be allowed to decide which journalists are able to cover the president based on the content of their news coverage.”

webTitle: Hispanic voters’ support for Trump wanes over economy and immigration

fields.headline: Hispanic voters’ support for Trump wanes over economy and immigration
fields.trailText: Polls show voters who helped elect president unhappy – and may be willing to vote Democrat in midterms
fields.bodyText: Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Donald Trump in 2024 are discontented with his second-term economic and immigration policies, according to recent polling – indicating they may not be willing to support the president’s party in the midterm elections. Despite a record number of Hispanic voters casting their ballots for the Republican president, more than 65% said they are displeased with Trump’s handling of his job and 78% said they would prefer to see the Democratic party in control of Congress, according to a September poll from the New York Times/Siena University. “When we ask voters, ‘OK, what is shaping your opinion about the president?’ The cost of living was number one, number two was immigration enforcement and deportation in US cities, number three is back to the economy – wages,” Clarissa Martinez De Castro, the vice-president of the Latino Vote Initiative at UnidosUS, said. Frustration with the consequences of the administration’s current policies are driving Latino voters away from Republicans, said Mike Madrid, a campaign consultant, author and teacher who has been studying Latino voting patterns for 35 years. “There’s no renewed affinity or love for the Democratic party. They’re just extremely upset and disillusioned and angry, frankly, with Donald Trump,” Madrid said. “So they’re gonna leave the Republicans for the exact same reasons that they left the Democrats two years ago,” he added. Other polls support those findings. Approximately 63% of Hispanic respondents told a Fox News survey in September they plan to vote for the Democratic congressional candidate in their district. In an UnidosUS poll from April/May, 54% of Hispanic voters said they would vote for the Democratic House candidate, compared with 27% who said they would favor the Republican. The economy and cost of living are top concerns for Hispanic voters, polls show. Trump’s message of economic populism helped him get elected in 2024, but voters, including Republicans, have soured on his handling of the economy amid high inflation and rising costs. The Iran war has pushed gas prices past $4 per gallon on average. Inflation has risen over the last year and remained stubborn at 3.4%, elevating grocery costs. When asked about the recent polling of Hispanic voters, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said “hard-working Hispanic Americans are beginning to have some breaking room after four year of economic pain under the Democrats” and pointed to policies such as middle-class tax cuts, no tax on tips, overtime and social security and “defeating Biden’s inflation crisis”. Schuster said Trump was “honored to receive a record level of support from Hispanic Americans that helped fuel his landslide 2024 election victory” and that the president and Republicans in Congress would “continue fighting to make everyday life more affordable for working families”. Between October 2025 and May 2026, Hispanic voters’ favorability of Democrats in Congress increased by three percentage points, according to UnidosUS’s bipartisan poll of 3,000 Hispanic voters. Meanwhile, favorability toward Republicans in Congress only increased by one percentage point. Immigration is also an issue, especially since the Trump administration has deployed federal agents to Latino and Hispanic communities across the country. Some who have encountered immigration agents have accused the administration of racial profiling to target immigrants for deportation. But immigration is not the biggest issue for Latino voters – a misconception that politicians often make. In UnidosUS’s poll of 3,000, 17% said they wanted elected officials to prioritize increasing border security. Another 13% said they supported deporting all undocumented immigrants, regardless of how long they have been in the US. Those who voted for Trump are part of a larger cohort of “swing” voters who have no allegiance to a specific political party. They make up roughly 40% of the Hispanic electorate and are often misunderstood by politicians, Martinez said. “You have 40% of voters here for whom, many of them say, they don’t see the difference between the parties in terms of who really is going to be better,” Martinez said of the group. “That tells candidates: you have homework to do, and the clock is ticking,” she added. Republicans and Democrats have long struggled to resonate with Latino voters, Madrid said, in part because politicians often assume they know exactly what Latino voters want without doing proper outreach. “The political structure has done a massive disservice with fake polling, with organizations that were advocating an agenda, not facts and science … and politicians that were trying to benefit from that,” Madrid, who has consulted for both Republican and Democratic campaigns, said. Madrid and Martinez cautioned that while Latino voters appear tofavor Democratic candidates ahead of the November elections, it does not mean Democrats can – or should – count on their support in 2028. “Latino voters themselves are changing, which is why the Latino vote has changed,” Madrid said. “And you can’t you can’t come up with a solution until you understand that.”

webTitle: Revenge of the labor movement: Democrats with union backgrounds aim to retake Congress

fields.headline: Revenge of the labor movement: Democrats with union backgrounds aim to retake Congress
fields.trailText: Meet the candidates with labor ties vying for Senate and House seats in midterm races. Most of the nominees are Democrats as the party looks to rebuild support among working-class voters
fields.bodyText: The US labor movement is having a banner election year. More than three dozen nominees for open House and Senate races across the US have backgrounds as labor union representatives or members. Several nominees are running in heavily blue districts, making it almost certain they will win the seat in November’s midterms, while others are in highly contested races that are likely to determine control of the House and possibly the Senate. Most are Democrats, though some are running as independents. The early success of so many candidates with ties to labor comes as Democrats work to rebuild their support among working-class voters, centering their campaign messaging around affordability issues. But the messenger matters, too. “In a political environment that’s been dominated by wealthy elites for decades, union candidates provide a level of trust and credibility that’s simply unmatched,” Steve Smith, a spokesperson for the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, told the Guardian. “These candidates are at long last returning the levers of power to the people.” A 2024 study by Cal State and UCLA researchers found working-class voters are 6.4 percentage points more likely to prefer a political candidate with a working-class occupation over one with an upper-class occupation. Yet a 2026 report by the Center for Working-Class Politics found working-class candidates make up just 8-14% of Democratic and 5-8% of Republican congressional candidates. Union candidates invoked pro-worker themes 159% more than non-union candidates, the report found. Running more union members as candidates, its authors argued, could increase the representation ordinary Americans have in Congress, by elevating people who can speak to and deliver on issues that affect the working class. “Voters want elected leaders who understand the struggles working people face in an economy rigged against us,” Smith said. “In every area of the country, at every level, union members are running for office and winning because they bring lived experience in leveling the playing field for workers and creating a brighter future for our families.” Americans overwhelmingly favor labor unions, according to recent annual Gallup polls, with 68% approving labor unions in 2025. But union density has been on a decline in recent decades, from more than 30% in the 1950s to 10% in 2025, correlating to a drastic increase in wealth and income inequality in the US. In 2024, Donald Trump sought to woo labor leaders and blue-collar voters with populist trade promises. But exit polls and surveys conducted after the presidential election found little evidence that union members had shifted toward Trump. According to the VoteCast survey conducted for the Associated Press and Fox News after the 2024 election, union members preferred Harris over Trump by 16% in 2024, 57% to 41% for Trump, matching Biden’s 16% lead over Trump with union households in 2020. Trump was formerly a union member, but he resigned from the Screen Actors Guild in February 2021 rather than facing disciplinary charges from the union for violating its constitution regarding his actions and role in inciting the attack on the US Capitol on 6 January 2021. In his resignation letter, Trump wrote “Who cares!” and accused the union of never doing anything for him. In response to his resignation, the union issued a two-word statement: “Thank you.” Meet the Senate and House candidates identified as having labor union backgrounds who are running to join the roughly 25 current members of Congress who have previously worked in the labor movement or in a job represented by a union. *** Todd Achilles Candidate for US Senate, Idaho Independent Todd Achilles, a former American Federation of Teachers member from his work as a public policy professor and lecturer, is running for the US Senate in a race where the Democratic nominee withdrew in July. *** Abdul El-Sayed Candidate for US Senate, Michigan Abdul El-Sayed is a former American Association of University Professors member and other higher education unions from his time working as a professor and scholar at Columbia University, Harvard University, the University of Michigan, Wayne State University and American University. The union made its first ever national political endorsement in endorsing his Senate campaign. In an interview with the Guardian in July, El-Sayed explained his critique of the economy and the impact of concentrated corporate power. “If the markets actually worked the way they’re supposed to, you might have some efficient movement of money,” he said. “The problem is, we don’t live in capitalism, we live in oligopoly.” *** Troy Jackson Candidate for US Senate, Maine Troy Jackson worked several past union jobs as a member of the unions of Painters and Allied Trades (IUPAT), the Machinists (IAM), Operating Engineers (IUOE), United Auto Workers (UAW), and Laborers’ International Union of North America (Liuna). “Everything Troy fights for comes from his working-class roots as a logger from Allagash and the 1998 blockade, when he stood up to powerful landowners undercutting Maine workers,” Jackson’s campaign spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, said in a statement. Gottlieb added: “Mainers know whose side Troy is on: theirs. For him, solidarity isn’t a slogan – it’s how he’s lived his life.” *** Angie Nixon Candidate for US Senate, Florida Angie Nixon is a state legislator in Florida and the Democratic nominee for Senate in a special election to fill Marco Rubio’s vacated seat. She previously has worked as a union organizer, directing the Florida Public Services Union’s (FPSU) higher education campaign. *** Dan Osborn Candidate for US Senate, Nebraska Dan Osborn, a former president of Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers and Grain Millers International Union (BCTGM) Local 50G, which represents Kellogg’s workers, is running for the US Senate in Nebraska as an independent. He faces Republican Pete Ricketts, the heir to billionaire Joe Ricketts, co-founder of TD Ameritrade. *** James Talarico Candidate for US Senate, Texas As a public school teacher, James Talarico was a member of the San Antonio Alliance of Teachers and Support Personnel. He is also a longtime member of the Texas State Employees Union (TSEU – CWA Local 6186). *** Colin Allred Candidate for Texas’s 33rd congressional district The former congressman Colin Allred is running again this cycle in a newly redrawn Democratic-dominant district in Texas. He is a former member of the NFL Players Association, the union representing National Football League players. Chris Backemeyer Candidate for Nebraska’s first congressional district Chris Backemeyer, a former US state department employee and the Democratic nominee for Nebraska’s first congressional district, is a member of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Local 1534. Mitchell Berman Candidate for Wisconsin’s first congressional district Mitchell Berman worked a union job in college at UPS, where he was a member of Teamsters Local 344. As a nurse, he has worked several union jobs including as a member of the Wisconsin Federation of Nurses & Health Professionals and National Nurses United. “Coming from a working-class background, understanding what folks are going through [and] having walked a mile in my neighbor’s shoes gives me the ability to look at legislation from the perspective of having some empathy and understanding for what people are dealing with,” Berman said in August. *** Bob Brooks Candidate for Pennsylvania’s seventh congressional district Bob Brooks, a former president of the Pennsylvania Professional Fire Fighters Association, is running to flip one of the state’s swing districts. “We need to change who’s representing us and who’s making the rules and the laws,” Brooks said in June. “That’s what inspired me to do this. I think we need more everyday people down there, because everyday people are the ones that are struggling.” *** Connie Chan Candidate for California’s 11th congressional district A former member of the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE) Local 21, Connie Chan is in a general election runoff to replace Nancy Pelosi’s vacated seat in California’s 11th congressional district. *** Darializa Avila Chevalier Candidate for New York’s 13th congressional district In one of the biggest primary upsets in 2026, Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated Adriano Espaillat, the incumbent congressman and chair of the Congressional Hispanic caucus, and she is expected to easily win the general election in a district that leans heavily in favor of Democrats. She is a union member of the United Auto Workers Local 2325. “That really changed the course of my education and my PhD program, to be able to be part of a union that fought for me, my work conditions, my wage, and made it possible for me to continue my program,” she said in June, reflecting on her experience joining the union. “I was able to teach at a pace that was manageable, right, with a workload that was manageable, but also be paid enough to actually lead a dignified life.” *** Carmela Conroy Candidate for Washington’s fifth congressional district Carmela Conroy was a union member represented by the American Foreign Service Association. *** Sam Forstag Candidate for Montana’s at-large congressional district Sam Forstag served as the vice-president of the Forest Service Council Local 60, an arm of the National Federation of Federal Employees. “There is genuinely a fundamental lack of representation for working people in federal office right now, and that has serious, substantive effects on what kind of policies they actually prioritize and what they pass,” Forstag said in February. “The primary function of government is to step in when the market is not meeting a need and to make people’s lives materially better. And it seems like some people at the national level forgot about that.” *** Chris Gallant Candidate for New York’s first congressional district Chris Gallant served as the president of his local union with the National Air Traffic Controllers Association. *** Vince George Candidate for West Virginia’s first congressional district Vince George was a member of the West Virginia Education Association and is a retired union member of American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (Afscme). *** Bob Harvie Candidate for Pennsylvania’s first congressional district A teacher for more than 20 years, Bob Harvie is a former member of the Bucks County Technical High School Education Association. *** Missi Hesketh Candidate for Missouri’s seventh congressional district Missi Hesketh is a teacher and a member the National Education Association and a former member of the Missouri State Teachers Association. *** Bill Hill Candidate for Alaska’s at-large congressional district Bill Hill, an independent, is a former union construction worker. The leading Democrat in the race dropped out and endorsed his campaign. *** Amanda Hollowell Candidate for Georgia’s first congressional district Amanda Hollowell was the state director for 9to5 in Georgia, a worker-led organization that arose from women-led worker organizing in the 1970s. *** Jake Johnson Candidate for Minnesota’s first congressional district A high school math teacher, Jake Johnson served as an official with his local teachers’ union. “To me, a lot of the great things that happen in public schools happen because of unions. We’re the ones fighting for smaller class sizes. We’re the ones fighting for reasonable wages,” Johnson said in July. “That’s happening because of teachers’ unions. We’re the ones that are raising the bar as far as teacher quality.” *** Tanya Lloyd Candidate for Texas’s 27th congressional district Tanya Lloyd is a former union member of the Texas American Federation of Teachers. *** Donavan McKinney Candidate for Michigan’s 13th congressional district A former organizer with the Service Employees International Union, Donavan McKinney defeated incumbent representative Shri Thanedar in the Democratic primary and is expected to easily win the district that favors Democrats by 22 percentage points, according to Cook Political Report’s Partisan Voting Index. *** Analilia Mejia Candidate for New Jersey’s 11th congressional district Analilia Mejia, who won a special election in New Jersey’s 11th congressional district in April, is a former union organizer with the Service Employees International Union, Unite Here, and United Food and Commercial Workers. *** Jena Nelson Candidate for Oklahoma’s fifth congressional district The former Oklahoma teacher of the year in 2020, Jena Nelson is a teachers’ union member. The district last flipped blue under Trump’s first term in 2018, but Republicans took back the district in 2020. *** Richard Pan Candidate for California’s sixth congressional district Richard Pan, a pediatrician, is a member of the Union of American Physicians and Dentists – Afscme Local 206. *** Brian Poindexter Candidate for Ohio’s seventh congressional district An ironworker, apprenticeship instructor and former organizer, Brian Poindexter is running to unseat Max Miller, the congressman who is facing calls to resign due to domestic assault allegations from his ex-wife, the daughter of Republican senator Bernie Moreno, and similar allegations made against him by Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary under Trump’s first administration. “People are working harder and harder. We’re getting less and less and we’re getting more and more of the burden,” Poindexter said. “I’d like to see an economy that works for all of us, not just the wealthy. We need to build an economy that rewards work, not just wealth.” *** Chris Rabb Candidate for Pennsylvania’s third congressional district Chris Rabb helped organize adjuncts at Temple University with the United Academics of Philadelphia, while he worked as an adjunct professor at the university. *** Kyle Rable Candidate for Texas’s 19th congressional district Kyle Rable is a member of the Texas State Employees Union, CWA Local 6186. *** Lauren Reinhold Candidate for Kansas’s first congressional district A former federal employee, Lauren Reinhold served as a union steward and officer while working at the Social Security Administration and National Labor Relations Board (NLRB). *** Ceretta Smith Candidate for Georgia’s 12th congressional district Ceretta Smith is a past president and current member of AFGE Local 2017 and also serves as the fair practices coordinator and women’s coordinator for AFGE Council 172, which represents Defense Commissary Agency workers. The US army veteran has worked as federal employee for more than 20 years. *** Katy Padilla Stout Candidate for Texas’s 23rd congressional district Katy Padilla Stout is a former teachers’ union member with the American Federation of Teachers, which has endorsed her campaign. *** Trina Swanson Candidate for Minnesota’s eighth congressional district Trina Swanson was a member of the American Federation of Government Employees while she worked at US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). She is running against the Republican incumbent representative, Pete Stauber. “Northern Minnesota taught her that unions strengthen our middle class,” Swanson’s campaign website states. *** Claire Valdez Candidate for New York’s seventh congressional district Claire Valdez won the Democratic primary for New York’s seventh congressional district after the retirement of Nydia Velázquez. Valdez served as an organizer with United Auto Workers Local 2110 at Columbia University. *** Mai Vang Candidate for California’s seventh congressional district A union member of the California Faculty Association, progressive Mai Vang edged past the 82-year-old Democratic incumbent Doris Matsui in the primary for California’s seventh congressional district. They will face each other again in the November general election. *** Randy Villegas Candidate for California’s 22nd congressional district Randy Villegas is a former United Auto Workers Local 4811 member, which represents higher-education workers. *** Brandon Wade Candidate for Oklahoma’s second congressional district Brandon Wade is an official with International Union of Operating Engineers Local 351, where he has held several different roles while working more than 20 years in the oil and gas industry. *** Justin Wagner Candidate for Pennsylvania’s 16th congressional district Justin Wagner is the Democratic nominee in Pennsylvania’s 16th congressional district, where he is running against incumbent Republican Mike Kelly. Wagner is a previous member of the United Auto Workers and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. *** Marni von Wilpert Candidate for California’s 48th congressional district Marni Von Wilpert is a former NLRB attorney who helped write the comprehensive labor law reform legislation, the Protecting the Right to Organize (Pro) Act, and a member of the Nonprofit Professional Employees Union while working at the Economic Policy Institute. “One of my biggest priorities for running for Congress myself is to finish this work, to come back as a member of Congress and finally get labor law reform across the finish line,” von Wilpert said. Her Republican opponent, Jim Desmond, worked as a pilot for Delta Air Lines, where he was a member of the pilots’ union, Air Line Pilots Association, but has opposed unions on project labor agreements.

webTitle: Kevin Warsh may be the adult in the room. But can he calm the US economy?

fields.headline: Kevin Warsh may be the adult in the room. But can he calm the US economy?
fields.trailText: Fed chair presided over unanimous decision to raise interest rates despite intense campaign from White House
fields.bodyText: In the end, Kevin Warsh’s Federal Reserve acquitted itself well. For all the uncertainty he had sparked at the previous meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, when he refused to provide any indication of what he was prepared to do to tame stubborn inflation, the chair on Wednesday presided over a unanimous decision to raise interest rates for the first time in three years. “Today’s action starts to show that we’re serious about this,” he said at the press conference after the meeting, with “this” meaning inflation in excess of the Fed’s 2% target for over five years. Welcome though it was, his embrace of economic orthodoxy nonetheless did little to dispel the Keystone Cops quality of governance in Donald Trump’s US. Warsh’s resolve – raising rates just a few weeks before elections that will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress – appeared even more resolute in the face of a veiled threat from White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett, who pointed out to his chums on Fox that “if you want an independent Fed, then one thing the Fed does is it stays out of the way of elections”. The central bankers’ parsimonious comments in the press conference following the meeting made a sharp contrast with the more unhinged commentary from other members of the administration, including the president himself, who earlier this month celebrated the resilience of the labor market with a mind-boggling threat to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” unless the Fed cut interest rates. Trump has yet to turn on Warsh in the way he did on his predecessor, Jerome “numbskull” Powell. But the signs are ominous. After the rate hike, Trump went ballistic – spewing more of the random, incoherent thoughts that have become his trademark. “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World,” he wrote on social media, despite recalcitrant inflation and a budget deficit that is likely to exceed $2tn this year. He again demanded the powers that be to “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” Yet more significant than the contrast between Warsh’s words and the incongruent economic rhetoric from the White House is the tension between the Fed’s decision on Wednesday and pretty much every other initiative from the administration, from the volley of tariffs against imports from everywhere to the war in Iran to Trump’s “promise” of $5,000 a head if he wins the midterms to treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s desperate efforts to pull interest rates down even as the Fed is raising them. All things considered, financial markets reacted relatively calmly to the day’s events. For sure, the S&P 500 index took a nosedive on Wednesday afternoon, closing some 0.4% lower at the thought that the Fed would likely now raise rates again in December and twice in 2027. The yield on the 10-year bond rose sharply, again surpassing 5%. But investors appear to have bought – for now at least – that whatever deranged policies may emerge from the rest of the administration, monetary policy will remain comparatively sane. Investors should probably remain on their toes, though. A rational Trump would probably thank Warsh for his hawkishness. There might be a plausible argument to keep rates where they were because inflation is driven by temporary forces, like a war. Yet had the Fed staid its hand, or – goodness forbid – cut rates as the president has demanded, the bloodbath in the treasury market would have been gruesome, as investors were forced to accept that the chair of the central bank would not stand up to the nut who appointed him. By contrast, by raising rates and demonstrating he is serious about curbing inflation, the Fed is likely to calm market jitters and reduce long-term inflation expectations, which will ultimately redound in lower yields on treasury bonds, allowing for lower interest rates on mortgages and other long-term loans that matter to businesses and consumers. More clown cars are likely on the way. In his fury on Wednesday, Trump again threatened to stop trading with countries that have a surplus with the US – a proposition so devoid of sense that it is hard to comprehend, let alone critique. The war in Iran is likely to continue throughout the administration, bringing more volatility to energy markets. Even Bessent seems to be losing his hold on reality. Vexed over rising treasury yields – which are raising the cost of servicing the government’s Brobdingnagian debts – the man whom markets believed would play the role of adult in the Oval Office on matters of economic policy has started to emulate the desperate government officials he once pummelled into submission. Bessent built a reputation in financial circles in 1996 as part of the team built by George Soros and Stanley Druckenmiller that pushed the British pound out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. They made a tidy profit by teaching hapless British ministers that however many pounds they bought to defend the exchange rate, they could never overcome a market determined to sell. Today, Bessent has taken the losing side of that trade, betting that he can buy enough treasuries to bring long-term interest rates down. The Fed on Wednesday likely helped Bessent’s cause. Still, the peculiar image of a central bank raising interest rates while the treasury secretary resorts to gunslinger tactics to lower them won’t restore trust in the creditworthiness of the United States. (“I am the house,” he proclaimed, hoping to achieve a steely gaze, rhetorically twirling and reholstering his revolver. “You can bet against me if you want.”) Can an unexpectedly solid Fed chair stabilize the ship of an American economy discombobulated by slapstick policymaking? Here’s hoping. But holding one’s breath may be a bad idea. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

webTitle: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario

fields.headline: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
fields.trailText: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
fields.bodyText: When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm. Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up. “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned. The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech. In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing. AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy. As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”. Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article. Amodei’s worst China fears Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China. Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers. “Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”. Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”. “There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology. Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.) But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount. Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements. “The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China. Amodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”. Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US. “There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said at a Politico event on Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.” Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy. “It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.” Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, with OpenAI hiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation. “There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.” Silicon Valley’s China hawks Although Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley. Several of the tech figures focused on China have connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology. Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper. “Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024. The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”. Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI. “A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns. Nuclear considered an option Some leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium. “Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowsky wrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay. Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei. Other China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027. Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win. “We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karp told Axios last year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.” The view from China While Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest. As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern. “They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda. China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei, accusing him of running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI. “Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.” A race to the bottom While the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s models hacking into outside organizations have become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI. “You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission. Although experts and diplomats have expressed little hope that upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it. “We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

webTitle: ‘It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment’: criticism mounts over Trump’s media ban - as it happened

fields.headline: ‘It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment’: criticism mounts over Trump’s media ban - as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump’s contentious Oval Office exchange with reporters in the Oval Offcie was dominated by questions, and tetchy answers, about his decision to punish three news outlets that were not allowed to be there: CNN, Politico and MS Now. Reminded that he tried to ban a CNN reporter from the White House in his first term, and lost in court, Trump said: “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day”. In his comments, he made it plan that his real beef with the outlets was that their coverage of him was not sufficiently flattering. “I get I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox,” Trump said. “It’s sick, I mean, there’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” the president said. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine. But I don’t have to let them into my- into the people’s house.” At another stage in the chaotic news conference, Trump was asked about how his banning of the three outlets from the White House would work. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban?” Trump asked. After an NBC News correspondent rephrased the question, Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” Trump’s threatened annexation of Greenland appears to be off the table, as the US president and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland announced that they expect to sign an Arctic security pact next week that might just reiterate the existing access the US has to Greenland through Nato. Donald Trump’s contentious Oval Office exchange with reporters on Friday was dominated by questions, and tetchy answers, about his decision to punish three news outlets that were not there – CNN, Politico and MS Now – for their unflattering coverage of his performance as president by banning them not just from the room, but from the White House. The impromptu half-hour news conference was also a demonstration of the extent to which the president has already exerted control over the way he is covered on live television by selecting which outlets are allowed in to the Oval Office, and who he calls on to ask him questions. That dynamic was on display throughout the event, as Trump repeatedly hectored reporters from nonpartisan outlets who asked him challenging questions and called on reporters from partisan, rightwing outlets who helped him steer the conversation away from his attack on press freedom and back to attacks on Democrats, culture war issues and boasts about his record. Trump clearly knew where the friendly faces in the room where, calling first on Daniel Baldwin of the far-right fringe cable channel One American News, who invited the president to criticize Democrats, and later moved away from being pressed on the media bans by Danny Kemp of AFP by calling on Willie Nelson of the rightwing outlet Salem Media. Nelson asked Trump to comment on the Lindsay Clancy trial and then invited him to riff on Hasan Piker, the left-wing streamer Republicans are trying to use to paint Democrats as extremists. When reporters like Catherine Lucey of the Wall Street Journal tried to bring the subject back to the president’s assault on the first amendment, Trump was scathing. “Freedom of the press is enshrined in the first amendment-”, Lucey began. “Oh, thank you for telling … thank you for telling me that, appreciate it,” Trump cut in. “Are you trying to intimidate the press from doing its job?” Lucey asked. “No, no, no, no. I dislike dishonest press like you. I think you’re terrible,” Trump replied, before calling on a reporter for the conservative Washington Examiner. When she returned to the subject of the ban, reminding Trump that he “tried a similar ban against CNN, and it didn’t survive a court challenge” in his first term, Trump gave a rambling answer that resulted in a frank admission that he was simply peeved by negative coverage. “I don’t get fair press,” he complained. “I get it from Breitbart. I get it from a little bit from Fox.” After scolding the NBC News correspondent Kelly O’Donnell for supposedly just asking Joe Biden what his favorite flavor of ice cream was (which O’Donnell said she never did), Trump said in response to another question that the outlets he banned on Friday simply “never write a good story” about him. “I won’t get a good story out of these people,” he added. Then, looking first in the direction of Baldwin, the One America News correspondent, and then at Nelson, of Salem Media, and pointing at each in turn Trump said: “From some of them I will. I’ll get one from him. I’ll get one from him.” “I’ll get a few of them, but it’s sick. I mean, there’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Trump said. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine. But I don’t have to let them into my- into the people’s house.” Statements continue to roll in from press freedom groups on Donald Trump’s move on Friday to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House for the grave crime of not producing sufficiently flattering coverage of him the president. Here is some of what Seth Stern, chief of advocacy of the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement: It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move. The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public. “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the First Amendment works,” Tim Richardson, journalism and disinformation director at PEN America chimed in. “As we’ve seen time and time again, this administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions. The White House can’t be allowed to decide which journalists are able to cover the president based on the content of their news coverage.” Aaron Terr, the director of public advocacy for the Foundation for Individual Rights in Education said: When the White House opens its doors to the press, it must comply with the First Amendment. The president is as free as any other person to criticize media coverage. But he can’t ban outlets from the White House just because he doesn’t like their reporting or commentary. Press credentials aren’t a reward for loyalty to the government. A free, even adversarial, press is a sign of our country’s strength. The public deserves to hear about its government from independent voices, not just its leader’s loyalists and allies. While the scope of the new security agreement announced on Friday by the leaders of the United States, Denmark and Greenland seems certain to fall far short of Donald Trump’s previously stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”, a Trump administration insider dropped a strong hint that the US side intends to present whatever the deal actually is as an American triumph. After news of the agreement broke, Katie Miller, a former White House aide in the first Trump administration whose husband is Trump’s most influential adviser, posted a map of Greenland entirely covered in the American flag, with the caption: “ITS [sic] HAPPENING”. On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins. The speakers included a drag queen while among the demonstrators were people in inflatable animal costumes and a man in a golden Trump mask with a crown and a sign that said: “Restore my name in gold you sycophants.” Another man wore a blue hat that said: “Make America intelligent again.” Baby Trump balloons danced in the air against the setting sun. Protesters beat drums, chanted “hands off!” and waved signs including: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Donny you are no JFK!”; “Kennedy Center 4 ever”; “Our center not DJT’s”; “Hands off the arts”; and “Wicked starring DJT”. Speaking Friday at Colgate University in Hamilton, New York, former president Barack Obama briefly reacted to Trump banning Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House due to their coverage of his administration. “I’m trying to think what would have happened if I’d said, you know what Fox News, get out of here,” Obama said. “It’s unimaginable.” Fox News aired relentless negative coverage of Obama’s two terms in office, regularly promoting the birther conspiracy and catering coverage to the fears of white conservatives, but always maintained a seat in the White House briefing room. Senator John Curtis, a Utah Republican, said on Friday that Donald Trump Jr’s wedding celebration in the Bahamas being paid for, in part, by a Russian boxing official close to the Kremlin, “just stinks – it’s corruption”. In a social media review of the week’s highs and lows, Curtis said: “inflation has worsened, I think we all have to admit that. Another low, believe this: a Russian oligarch paid for a lavish wedding afterparty for Donald Trump Jr, which, to me, it just stinks – it’s corruption.” “I don’t like it,” Curtis added, before hinting that he might soon have more to say on the topic. “I want to be careful because I don’t want to just talk about this passively. You’ll hear more from me later on. This is a big deal.” Donald Trump plans to meet next week with Delcy Rodríguez, who became president after a US military raid in January captured then-leader Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face drug trafficking charges. Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations, told reporters that Trump and Rodriguez will take part in what’s known as a “pull-aside” meeting – a more casual meeting than a formal bilateral sit-down – during the United Nations general assembly in New York City. Trump will meet with the new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, for the first time, according to Waltz, who as Trump’s national security adviser until he mistakenly added the editor of the Atlantic magazine to a private Signal group chat in which the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, briefed senior officials, including the vice-president, JD Vance, on planned strikes on Houthi rebels in Yemen. The Iran-backed rebels Yemeni fighters recently seized control of the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the strait of Hormuz. Trump also plans to meet the leaders of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain, which are on the front lines of the war he started with Iran nearly seven months ago. The first meeting between Trump and Rodríguez, who had been Maduro’s vice-president, comes after the two countries announced an agreement last month to give the US a stake in Venezuela’s oil reserves. In response to Donald Trump’s move to bar CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, Jacqui Heinrich, who covers the president for Fox News, points out that Trump himself referred to his action as a “ban on the free press”. Here is the full statement from Heinrich, on behalf of the organization that recently made the US president the featured speaker at its annual dinner celebrating press freedom, where he congratulated and then trashed reporters who covered his chaotic presidency: The president said it plainly in the Oval Office, describing his own planned action as a “ban on the free press.” The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference. That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask. This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office. The WHCA stands in defense of our colleagues at CNN, MSNOW, and Politico who are being singled out for doing their jobs. Donald Trump on Friday signed legislation enabling sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it into ending its war with Ukraine, and also giving him the power to impose additional tariffs on countries breaking the embargo. The US president signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law two days after it passed the House of Representatives in a bipartisan 262-159 vote, amid concerns the legislation gives him too much power. The legislation imposes new sanctions on Russian political and military officials and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. In addition, it targets Russia’s fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite existing sanctions on its energy exports. But it also gives Trump wide leeway over its implementation, including which countries could face tariffs, and which tariff rates could be imposed. It also gives him sweeping discretion over whether sanctions provisions can be waived against certain countries. Controversially, it allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on buyers of Russian energy, including China, and on other countries that help Moscow to evade sanctions. The bill’s broad provisions were criticized by many Democrats, who complained that it gave Trump excessive authority to resort to tariffs, which he has already imposed on multiple countries despite a US supreme court ruling prohibiting him from doing so under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Donald Trump’s threatened annexation of Greenland appears to be off the table, as the US president and the leaders of Denmark and Greenland announced on Friday that they expect to sign an Arctic security pact next week during the United Nations general assembly in New York City. Trump cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming on social media that the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”. “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added without mentioning that the US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato. Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”. The island is a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. Frederiksen said that what she called “a great agreement” for all three parties, “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. Nielsen said it was “joyous” that the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base. Near the end of a chaotic news conference in the Oval Office on Friday, when a reporter tried to bring Donald Trump back to the subject of his move to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, over unflattering coverage he referred to as “fake”, the president seemed to admit that what he is attempting to do is a violation of the freedom of the press enshrined in the US constitution. “On the ban, what does that mean in practice?” the reporter asked. “Are you taking away their badges? Are you banning them from the pool? What does this actually mean?” “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban?” Trump replied. “Do you know how many bans I’m involved in? I’ve got more bans going than any human being!” “On the three news outlets, sir, what does that mean in practice?” the reporter clarified. Looking genuinely confused, Trump said: “Wh- I still don’t know what she’s”, before turning for help to those around him. NBC News correspondent Kelly O’Donnell then rephrased the question, asking: “What do you envision the bans would look like on the media outlets?” Trump said: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” “Uh”, Trump said, “a very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can. And if they could straighten themselves out, you know, if they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it. Look, they’re very dishonest people. They write in a very dishonest way.” He then went on to give an inaccurate account of the settlements he extracted from ABC News and CBS News after suing them over coverage he objected to, and, not for the first time, falsely claimed that the BBC documentary on the January 6 2021 Capitol riot he has sued the corporation over used technology to put words in his mouth that he never actually said. “They put horrible fighting words into my mouth,” Trump claimed, incorrectly. “BBC actually changed my language and they put words in my mouth.” “We’ll be suing these people too,” he added, in apparent reference to the three outlets he banned from the White House on Friday. Here is a statement from Jameel Jaffer, the executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, on Donald Trump’s move to bar CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House for unflattering coverage of his work as president: The First Amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage, just as it prohibits him from punishing universities because he doesn’t like the courses they offer, or from punishing law firms because he doesn’t like the clients they represent. With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you’d think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now. If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a ‘public forum’ under the First Amendment, which means the president can’t exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints. “Donald Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done,” Chuck Schumer, the leader of the Senate Democrats posted in response to Trump’s move to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. Directly addressing Trump on social media, Schumer added: “this is a democracy.
